name: Legitimists
summary: Legitimists were the French royalists who, after the July Revolution of 1830, held that the crown belonged by hereditary right to the senior Bourbon line, and who opposed republicans, Orleanists and Bonapartists alike. Their claimant, the Count de Chambord, refused any compromise on the white flag and promised, in his 1871 manifesto, a government resting on administrative decentralisation and local franchises. The defining reference works record the dynastic claim, not a full programme on economics, society or the wider world.
scope: French Legitimism after 1830, as Britannica, the 1911 Britannica and Universalis define it (supporters of the senior Bourbon line as legitimate kings of France, 'by divine right'), with the Count de Chambord's 5 July 1871 manifesto as its primary text. It excludes the Orleanist and Bonapartist royalists, Ultra-royalism before 1830, later social-Catholic or corporatist writers whom no defining source ties to the name, and the Blancs d'Espagne beyond their dynastic claim.
